--- title: "In-Class Exercise 6" subtitle: "Emerging Hot Spot Analysis" author: "Le Truong Chinh" date: "3 October 2026" date-modified: "4 October 2026" description: "An ISSS626 in-class exercise tracing how GDP per capita hot and cold spots changed across Hunan from 2005 to 2016." title-block-banner: true page-layout: article toc: true toc-depth: 4 number-sections: true code-overflow: wrap format: html: code-fold: false execute: echo: true eval: true warning: false message: false freeze: true fig-align: center --- ::: {.exercise-lead} This exercise looks at where GDP per capita formed hot and cold spots in Hunan, and whether those patterns became stronger or weaker over time. ::: ## Overview Emerging Hot Spot Analysis combines two ideas. Local Gi\* identifies clusters of high or low values in each year, while the Mann-Kendall test checks whether those clusters show a steady trend through time. The analysis has four main steps: 1. Create a space-time cube. 2. Calculate local Gi\* for every county and year. 3. Test each county for an upward or downward trend. 4. Classify the resulting hot and cold spot patterns. ## Getting started ### Installing and Loading the R Packages The packages below handle the spatial data, space-time analysis, maps and interactive chart. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pacman::p_load(sf, sfdep, tmap, plotly, tidyverse, Kendall) ``` ::: ## The Data The Hunan boundary layer contains 88 counties. The attribute table records GDP per capita for each county from 2005 to 2016. ### Importing geospatial data The county boundaries are projected to EPSG 32650 so that distance-based calculations use metres. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hunan <- st_read( dsn = "data/geospatial", layer = "Hunan") %>% st_transform(crs = 32650) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Reading layer `Hunan' from data source `D:\smu\study\GIS\In-class_Ex\In-class_Ex06\data\geospatial' using driver `ESRI Shapefile' Simple feature collection with 88 features and 7 fields Geometry type: POLYGON Dimension: XY Bounding box: xmin: 108.7831 ymin: 24.6342 xmax: 114.2544 ymax: 30.12812 Geodetic CRS: WGS 84 ``` ::: ::: ### Importing attribute table ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} GDPPC <- read_csv( "data/aspatial/Hunan_GDPPC.csv") ``` ::: ## Creating a Time Series Cube The boundary and yearly GDP records are linked by county name. Each county-year combination becomes one observation in the cube. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} GDPPC_st <- spacetime(GDPPC, hunan, .loc_col = "County", .time_col = "Year") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} is_spacetime_cube(GDPPC_st) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: A `TRUE` result confirms that the county and yearly data form a valid space-time cube. ## Computing Gi\* ### Deriving the spatial weights Counties that share a boundary are treated as neighbours. Each county is also included as its own neighbour because Gi\* measures a county together with its surroundings. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} GDPPC_nb <- GDPPC_st %>% activate("geometry") %>% mutate(nb = include_self( st_contiguity(geometry)), wt = st_inverse_distance(nb, geometry, scale = 1, alpha = 1), .before = 1) %>% set_nbs("nb") %>% set_wts("wt") ``` ::: The same neighbour and weight structure is copied to every year. Row order must remain unchanged after this step. ## Computing Gi\* Local Gi\* is calculated separately for each year. A positive value points towards a cluster of high GDP per capita, while a negative value points towards a cluster of low GDP per capita. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gi_stars <- GDPPC_nb %>% group_by(Year) %>% mutate(gi_star = local_gstar_perm( GDPPC, nb, wt)) %>% tidyr::unnest(gi_star) ``` ::: ## Mann-Kendall Test The Mann-Kendall test checks for a consistent trend without assuming that the values follow a normal distribution. Tau is positive for an upward trend and negative for a downward trend. A p-value below 0.05 indicates a statistically significant trend. ### Mann-Kendall Test on Gi Changsha is used as a simple example before the test is repeated for all counties. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cbg <- gi_stars %>% ungroup() %>% filter(County == "Changsha") |> select(County, Year, gi_star) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = cbg, aes(x = Year, y = gi_star)) + geom_line() + theme_light() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](In_Class_Ex6_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Interactive Mann-Kendall Plot The same series can be explored interactively by moving over the line. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(data = cbg, aes(x = Year, y = gi_star)) + geom_line() + theme_light() ggplotly(p) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ### Printing Mann-Kendall test report ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cbg %>% summarise(mk = list( unclass( Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star)))) %>% tidyr::unnest_wider(mk) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 x 5 tau sl S D varS 1 0.485 0.00742 66 136. 589. ``` ::: ::: Here, `tau` gives the direction and strength of the trend, while `sl` is the p-value used to judge its significance. ### Mann-Kendall test data.frame The same test is now applied to every county. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ehsa <- gi_stars %>% group_by(County) %>% summarise(mk = list( unclass( Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star)))) %>% tidyr::unnest_wider(mk) head(ehsa) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 x 6 County tau sl S D varS 1 Anhua 0.191 0.303 26 136. 589. 2 Anren -0.294 0.108 -40 136. 589. 3 Anxiang 0 1 0 136. 589. 4 Baojing -0.691 0.000128 -94 136. 589. 5 Chaling -0.0882 0.650 -12 136. 589. 6 Changning -0.750 0.0000318 -102 136. 589. ``` ::: ::: ### Mann-Kendall test data.frame The table below brings the strongest and most statistically significant trends to the top. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} emerging <- ehsa %>% arrange(sl, abs(tau)) %>% slice(1:10) head(emerging) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 x 6 County tau sl S D varS 1 Shuangfeng 0.868 0.00000143 118 136. 589. 2 Xiangtan 0.868 0.00000143 118 136. 589. 3 Xiangxiang 0.868 0.00000143 118 136. 589. 4 Chengbu -0.824 0.00000482 -112 136. 589. 5 Dongan -0.824 0.00000482 -112 136. 589. 6 Wugang -0.809 0.00000712 -110 136. 589. ``` ::: ::: ## Performing Emerging Hotspot Analysis The full analysis combines the yearly Gi\* results with each county's trend. One time lag is used, with 99 simulations for the significance test. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ehsa <- emerging_hotspot_analysis( x = GDPPC_st, .var = "GDPPC", k = 1, nsim = 99 ) ``` ::: ### Visualising the distribution of EHSA classes ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data = ehsa, aes(x = classification)) + geom_bar() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](In_Class_Ex6_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Sporadic cold spots are the largest group, followed by sporadic hot spots. This means most detected counties move in and out of significance instead of remaining a hot or cold spot throughout the whole period. ### Visualising EHSA The EHSA results are joined to the county boundaries. Only classes with a p-value below 0.05 are coloured on the final map. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} hunan_ehsa <- hunan %>% left_join(ehsa, by = join_by(County == location)) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ehsa_sig <- hunan_ehsa %>% filter(p_value < 0.05) tmap_mode("plot") tm_shape(hunan_ehsa) + tm_polygons() + tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) + tm_shape(ehsa_sig) + tm_fill("classification") + tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.4) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](In_Class_Ex6_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The significant classes are spread across Hunan rather than forming one single part of the province. The map also supports the bar chart: sporadic patterns are much more visible than long-lasting ones. ### Interpretation of EHSA classes - **Persistent:** the county remained a statistically significant hot or cold spot for most of the period. - **Intensifying:** the spatial pattern became stronger over time. - **Diminishing:** the pattern remained present but became weaker. - **New:** the county became a hot or cold spot only near the end of the period. - **Sporadic:** the pattern appeared in some years but was not continuous. ## Takeaways Looking at one year alone would miss how the spatial pattern developed. Gi\* identifies where neighbouring counties share high or low GDP per capita in each year, while the Mann-Kendall test distinguishes a short-lived pattern from a consistent change through time. ## References - [Chapter 11: Emerging Hot Spot Analysis](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap11) - [Understanding Emerging Hotspots with sfdep](https://sfdep.josiahparry.com/articles/understanding-emerging-hotspots.html)
